title: Subtree of Another Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: serialization plus substring search versus a direct recursive same-tree check at every node.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given the roots of two binary trees, root and subRoot, return true if there exists a subtree of root that has the SAME structure and node values as subRoot.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root, subRoot (two binary tree roots)"],["Output","true if some node's entire subtree within root exactly matches subRoot"],["Goal","Visit every node of root, checking if its subtree structurally equals subRoot at each"],["Constraints","Up to 2000 nodes in root, up to 1000 in subRoot"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Does one tree appear as an exact subtree of another?\"","A recursive descent over root, checking at every visited node whether its full subtree structurally equals subRoot (a helper \"same tree\" comparison)"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

root contains subRoot as a subtree exactly when SOME node in root, together with everything beneath it, is structurally and value-wise IDENTICAL to subRoot. Checking this requires two nested ideas: a helper function that checks if two trees are exactly identical, and an outer traversal trying that helper at every node of root.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding an Exact Matching Branch Within a Larger Tree
blocks.text: Picture searching a large tree for a branch that, taken as its own standalone tree, is an exact match (same shape, same labels) to a given smaller sample tree. Every branching point of the large tree needs to be checked as a possible starting point for this exact match.

blocks.caption: Visit every node of root, checking if that node's entire subtree exactly equals subRoot

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: root = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2], subRoot = [4, 1, 2]
Result: true. The subtree rooted at node 4 (with children 1 and 2) matches subRoot exactly.
Example: root = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2, null, null, null, null, 0], subRoot = [4, 1, 2]
Result: false. Node 4's subtree now has an extra node (0 under 2), so it no longer exactly matches subRoot.
5. How Should We Think?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Checking if two ENTIRE trees are identical is a straightforward recursive comparison: both null (match), or both non-null with equal values and recursively identical left and right subtrees.

Observation 2: root contains subRoot as a subtree exactly when this "identical trees" check succeeds for SOME node of root paired with subRoot.

Observation 3: Trying this check at EVERY node of root (via a normal tree traversal) and returning true the moment any one succeeds directly answers the question.
This leads to two functions working together: isSameTree(a, b) for exact structural equality, and isSubtree(root, subRoot) which tries isSameTree at every node of root.
6. Brute Force Solution
Serialize both trees into strings (including markers for null children to disambiguate structure), then check if subRoot's serialized string appears as a substring of root's serialized string.
Why the code is written this way

items: Serializing and using substring search implements the definition cleverly, but indirectly.
This needs careful marker placement to avoid false positive substring matches, and relies on a separate substring-search algorithm; a direct recursive tree comparison avoids both concerns.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(size of root plus size of subRoot) for serialization, plus O(combined string lengths) for the substring search.
Space: O(size of root plus size of subRoot) for the serialized strings.
Limitation: a direct recursive comparison at every node of root avoids the string construction and substring-search machinery entirely.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Define isSameTree(a, b): both null is a match; exactly one null is not; otherwise, values must match AND both subtrees must recursively match. Define isSubtree(root, subRoot): if root is null, no match is possible, return false; otherwise, return true if isSameTree(root, subRoot) succeeds directly at this node, OR if subRoot is found within root's left subtree, OR within root's right subtree (tried recursively).
Use a direct recursive descent over root, trying an exact "same tree" comparison against subRoot at every visited node.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for root = [3,4,5,1,2], subRoot = [4,1,2]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node visited in root","isSameTree(node, subRoot)?"],"rows":[["3","no (root values 3 vs 4 differ)"],["4","YES, structure and values match exactly, return true"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Trying isSameTree at every single node of root (via the outer recursive traversal) guarantees that if ANY node's subtree exactly matches subRoot, it will be found, since every node is eventually visited; the recursive isSameTree helper correctly verifies both structure (matching null patterns) and values at every corresponding position.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(size of root times size of subRoot) worst case, since isSameTree can be attempted at every node of root, each costing up to O(size of subRoot).
Space: O(height of root) recursion depth.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Serialize plus substring search","O(combined sizes) roughly","O(combined sizes)","Clever, but relies on extra substring-search machinery."],["Direct recursive descent plus same-tree check","O(size of root times size of subRoot) worst case","O(height of root)","The expected, straightforward solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Subtree of Another Tree combines two nested recursive ideas cleanly: an exact "same tree" comparison, tried at every node during an outer traversal.
Common Mistakes

items: Checking only value equality at the current node without recursively verifying the FULL subtree structure and values match subRoot exactly.
Forgetting to also search root's left and right subtrees when the current node itself is not a match.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["subRoot equals root itself entirely","Matches trivially at the very first isSameTree check."],["subRoot is larger than any subtree of root","Correctly returns false, since isSameTree can never succeed."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "this needs both an exact-match helper AND an outer traversal trying that helper everywhere" clarifies the two-layer recursive structure needed.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "check if one tree appears as an exact subtree within another", think: a same-tree helper, tried at every node of the larger tree.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you speed this up using tree serialization with proper escaping, or hashing subtree structures (like a Merkle-tree style hash) to compare in O(1) per node instead of O(size of subRoot)?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Symmetric Tree and Same Tree, both build on the identical "same tree" recursive comparison used here as a helper.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches are efficient for the given constraints; the direct recursive descent with a same-tree helper is the simpler, more commonly expected interview solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a same-tree helper, tried at every node during an outer recursive traversal.
Core Idea: root contains subRoot exactly when some node's full subtree structurally and value-wise matches subRoot.
Time: O(size of root times size of subRoot) worst case for the direct approach.
Most Important Observation: two nested recursive ideas (exact match, and search everywhere) combine cleanly here.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, easy to medium recursive tree problem.
One line memory trick: exact match tried at every node.
